svg.title: What a convolution computes
svg.text: toy 5 × 5 image, one 3 × 3 vertical-edge kernel, no padding, stride 1

g.text: A convolution slides a small grid of weights (the kernel) over the image. Each stop gives one output number.
Window at column 0: multiply 9 pairs and add. (−1·0 + 0·0 + 1·1) × 3 rows = 3: the window's right column sits on the stroke.
Window at column 1: multiply 9 pairs and add. (−1·0 + 0·1 + 1·0) × 3 = 0: the stroke is under the kernel's middle (weight 0).
Window at column 2: multiply 9 pairs and add. (−1·1 + 0·0 + 1·0) × 3 = −3: the stroke is under the left column (weight −1).
The next rows give the same numbers. The map says "dark-to-light edge here" (+3) and "light-to-dark" (−3).
The SAME 9 weights are used at every position. That sharing is why conv1 needs only 6 filters × 5 × 5 = 150 weights.
LeNet conv1: 6 kernels of 5 × 5 on a 32 × 32 image → 6 maps of 28 × 28 (32 − 5 + 1 = 28). Learned, not hand-set.
